title: Supreme Court Says Marijuana User Can Own Guns—Here's Why
summary: Can you own a gun if you use marijuana? The U.S. Supreme Court just said yes—at least in some cases. The court ruled that the government was wrong to convict a Texas man named Ali Hemani for having a gun while using marijuana. In 2022, federal agents found a pistol and 60 grams of marijuana in his home. Hemani told them he uses marijuana "about every other day." A law says "unlawful" drug users can't have guns, but it doesn't explain what "unlawful user" means. Is it someone who uses once a year? Every six months? Hemani's lawyers argued the law is too vague, and the Supreme Court agreed. Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote that the decision is narrow—it doesn't mean all drug users can have guns. It also doesn't stop laws against gun ownership by felons or people who are drunk. Marijuana is legal in some form in over 40 states, and more than 15% of Americans 12 and older used it in 2024. Gun rights groups and civil liberties groups both supported Hemani. The government said the law is like old laws that stopped "habitual drunkards" from having guns, but the court said the current law isn't clear enough. This case is part of a bigger debate about gun rights after a major Supreme Court ruling in 2022.
why_it_matters: This case shows how courts make sure laws are clear and fair, and it might affect future gun rules for people who use marijuana, which is becoming legal in many states.

Article_Structure: WHO: Ali Hemani, a Texas man who used marijuana, and the U.S. Supreme Court, with Justice Neil Gorsuch writing the opinion
WHAT: The court said a law banning drug users from having guns was too vague to convict Hemani
WHERE: The case started in Texas, but the Supreme Court in Washington, D.C., made the final decision
WHY: Because the law did not clearly define who counts as an 'unlawful user,' so Hemani could not be found guilty

perspectives.description: Gun rights supporters and people who use marijuana for medical reasons may see this as a win, because it protects their rights.
Some people worry that allowing any drug user to have guns could be dangerous and make it harder to keep guns away from those who should not have them.
The ruling is narrow, so lawyers and lawmakers will now try to write clearer laws that still keep guns from risky people while protecting fair treatment.
